claim: CXCL10 is produced by pancreatic precancerous lesion cells in response to IFNγ signaling.
source: We show that CXCL10 is produced by pancreatic precancerous lesion cells in response to IFNγ signaling and that inflammatory macrophages are recipients for this chemokine.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing IFNγ-induced CXCL10 expression in SM3 cells (Figure 1C-E) and ISH showing CXCL10 in ADM and PanIN lesions (Figure 1A,B).

claim: Inflammatory macrophages are recipients for CXCL10.
source: We show that CXCL10 is produced by pancreatic precancerous lesion cells in response to IFNγ signaling and that inflammatory macrophages are recipients for this chemokine.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing CXCR3 expression in inflammatory macrophages (Figure 2A, 2D) and chemoattraction assays (Figure 2B).

claim: CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling in macrophages mediates their chemoattraction to the pancreas.
source: CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling in macrophages mediates their chemoattraction to the pancreas, enhances their proliferation, and maintains their inflammatory identity.
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell chemoattraction assays showing M1 macrophages migrate toward CXCL10 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling enhances macrophage proliferation.
source: CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling in macrophages mediates their chemoattraction to the pancreas, enhances their proliferation, and maintains their inflammatory identity.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract but specific proliferation data is not shown for peritoneal or bone marrow-derived macrophages, only negative data for tissue-resident macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling maintains inflammatory identity of macrophages.
source: CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling in macrophages mediates their chemoattraction to the pancreas, enhances their proliferation, and maintains their inflammatory identity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that blocking CXCR3 causes M1 macrophages to upregulate M2 markers (Figure 3A,B) and decreases inflammatory macrophages in vivo (Figure 3C,D).

claim: Blocking CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling in vivo shifts macrophage populations to a tumor-promoting (Ym1+, Fizz+, Arg1+) phenotype.
source: Blocking of CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling in vivo shifts macrophage populations to a tumor-promoting (Ym1+, Fizz+, Arg1+) phenotype, increases fibrosis, and mediates progression of lesions, highlighting the importance of this pathway in PDA development.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased Ym1+ macrophages after CXCR3 neutralization (Figure 4A,B) and upregulation of Ym1, Fizz1, and Arg1 in vitro (Figure 3B).

claim: Blocking CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling in vivo increases fibrosis.
source: Blocking of CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling in vivo shifts macrophage populations to a tumor-promoting (Ym1+, Fizz+, Arg1+) phenotype, increases fibrosis, and mediates progression of lesions, highlighting the importance of this pathway in PDA development.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased SMA content after CXCR3 neutralization (Figure 4C,D) and CXCL10 neutralization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).

claim: Blocking CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling in vivo mediates progression of pancreatic lesions.
source: Blocking of CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling in vivo shifts macrophage populations to a tumor-promoting (Ym1+, Fizz+, Arg1+) phenotype, increases fibrosis, and mediates progression of lesions, highlighting the importance of this pathway in PDA development.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased abnormal pancreatic area after CXCR3 neutralization (Figure 4E,F).

claim: Overexpression of CXCL10 in PanIN cells reverses the effects of CXCR3 blockade.
source: This is reversed when CXCL10 is overexpressed in PanIN cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that CXCL10 overexpression in SM3 cells implanted in nude mice decreased abnormal tissue area, fibrosis, and M2 macrophages while increasing M1 macrophages (Figure 5).

claim: CXCL10 is expressed in ADM and PanIN1 lesions of KC mice.
source: While Cxcl10 was undetectable in normal adjacent acini (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), we found significant expression of Cxcl10 in ADM and PanIN1 lesions (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH data showing Cxcl10 mRNA in ADM and PanIN lesions (Figure 1A,B).

claim: CXCL10 expression is approximately fivefold higher in ADM than in PanIN lesions.
source: Quantification analyses of samples stained for Cxcl10 mRNA by ISH indicated approximately fivefold higher expression in ADM than in PanIN (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of ISH staining (Figure 1B).

claim: Expression of KRasG12D is unable to increase Cxcl10 expression in primary acinar cells.
source: However, expression of KRasG12D was unable to increase Cxcl10 expression, indicating an external stimulus as a driver.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from acinar cells infected with Adeno-cre-GFP versus Adeno-null-GFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: IFNγ stimulation induces over 60-fold increase in Cxcl10 mRNA in SM3 cells.
source: Treatment of SM3 cells with IFNγ induced an over 60-fold increase in Cxcl10 mRNA (Figure 1C), as well as increased CXCL10 protein production (Figure 1D) and secretion (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 1C).

claim: IFNγ stimulation increases CXCL10 protein production in SM3 cells.
source: Treatment of SM3 cells with IFNγ induced an over 60-fold increase in Cxcl10 mRNA (Figure 1C), as well as increased CXCL10 protein production (Figure 1D) and secretion (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data (Figure 1D).

claim: IFNγ stimulation increases CXCL10 secretion in SM3 cells.
source: Treatment of SM3 cells with IFNγ induced an over 60-fold increase in Cxcl10 mRNA (Figure 1C), as well as increased CXCL10 protein production (Figure 1D) and secretion (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data from media supernatants (Figure 1E).

claim: IFNγ-induced CXCL10 expression is mediated through JAK-STAT1 signaling.
source: We found that IFNγ stimulation led to phosphorylation of STAT1 at Y701 (activating phosphorylation), increased expression of CXCL10, and that pre-treatment with NVP-BSK805 inhibited IFNγ-induced pY701-STAT1 and CXCL10 expression (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data showing that JAK inhibitor NVP-BSK805 blocks IFNγ-induced STAT1 phosphorylation and CXCL10 expression (Figure 1F).

claim: T cells and NK cells are potential sources for IFNγ in the pancreatic microenvironment of KC mice.
source: As expected from published data, we found both T cells and NK cells as a potential source for IFNγ (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH for Ifng combined with IHC for CD4, CD8, and NKG2D markers (Figure 1G) and is consistent with published literature.

claim: Non-polarized peritoneal macrophages express high levels of Cxcr3.
source: We found that non-polarized peritoneal macrophages express high levels of the CXCL10 receptor Cxcr3, while M1-polarized (inflammatory) macrophages express moderate levels, and M2-polarized (alternatively activated) macrophages do not express this receptor (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 2A).

claim: M1-polarized macrophages express moderate levels of Cxcr3.
source: We found that non-polarized peritoneal macrophages express high levels of the CXCL10 receptor Cxcr3, while M1-polarized (inflammatory) macrophages express moderate levels, and M2-polarized (alternatively activated) macrophages do not express this receptor (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 2A).

claim: M2-polarized macrophages do not express Cxcr3.
source: We found that non-polarized peritoneal macrophages express high levels of the CXCL10 receptor Cxcr3, while M1-polarized (inflammatory) macrophages express moderate levels, and M2-polarized (alternatively activated) macrophages do not express this receptor (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 2A).

claim: CXCL10 acts as a chemoattractant for M1-polarized macrophages.
source: Transwell invasion assays using both peritoneal and bone marrow-derived macrophages suggest that CXCL10 can act as a chemoattractant for M1-polarized macrophages (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell assay data (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Approximately 80% of tissue resident macrophages in normal mouse pancreas express CXCR3.
source: Approximately 80% of tissue resident macrophages in normal mouse pancreas express CXCR3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but when isolated, these cells do not proliferate in response to CXCL10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Isolated tissue resident macrophages do not proliferate in response to CXCL10.
source: Approximately 80% of tissue resident macrophages in normal mouse pancreas express CXCR3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but when isolated, these cells do not proliferate in response to CXCL10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by MTT proliferation assay data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Approximately 40% of pancreatic macrophages in KC mice express CXCR3.
source: We found that approximately 40% of pancreatic macrophages in KC mice express CXCR3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis of sorted CD3+ and F4/80+ cells (Figure 2C).

claim: Inflammatory (F4/80+;pY701-STAT1+) macrophages express CXCR3 in KC mice.
source: Moreover, an in situ IF-IHC analysis of pancreata of KC mice indicated that inflammatory (F4/80+;pY701-STAT1+) macrophages express CXCR3, while alternatively activated (F4/80+;Ym1+) macrophages do not express this receptor (Figure 2D), which also confirmed above in vitro data.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 2D).

claim: Alternatively activated (F4/80+;Ym1+) macrophages do not express CXCR3 in KC mice.
source: Moreover, an in situ IF-IHC analysis of pancreata of KC mice indicated that inflammatory (F4/80+;pY701-STAT1+) macrophages express CXCR3, while alternatively activated (F4/80+;Ym1+) macrophages do not express this receptor (Figure 2D), which also confirmed above in vitro data.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 2D).

claim: Approximately 70% of CXCR3+ cells are M1 macrophages in human patient tumors.
source: An overlay between an ISH for Cxcr3 and IF-IHC for inflammatory macrophages (CD68+;iNOS+) in human patient tumors showed that ~70% of CXCR3+ cells are M1 macrophages and confirmed this population as a potential recipient for CXCL10 (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH and IF-IHC overlay analysis in patient samples (Figure 2E,F).

claim: CXCR3 neutralization causes M1 macrophages to express Ym1.
source: We found that upon CXCR3 neutralization, M1 macrophages, although still iNOS positive, start to express Ym1 (Figure 3A), which we previously have identified as a bona fide marker for M2 alternatively activated macrophages in precancerous abnormal pancreas lesions (Bastea et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 3A) and previous citation.

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in M1 macrophages decreases CD38 expression.
source: A more thorough analysis using qRT-PCR indicated a significant decrease in CD38, which is a distinct M1 macrophage marker (Jablonski et al., 2015), and an upregulation of Ym1, Arg1 and Fizz1 (Figure 3B), which are all markers of the alternatively activated macrophage population that previously has been shown to drive fibrosis during pancreatic lesion progression (Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 3B) and citation to Jablonski et al., 2015.

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in M1 macrophages upregulates Ym1, Arg1, and Fizz1.
source: A more thorough analysis using qRT-PCR indicated a significant decrease in CD38, which is a distinct M1 macrophage marker (Jablonski et al., 2015), and an upregulation of Ym1, Arg1 and Fizz1 (Figure 3B), which are all markers of the alternatively activated macrophage population that previously has been shown to drive fibrosis during pancreatic lesion progression (Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 3B) and citation to Liou et al., 2017.

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in M1 macrophages increases Il4ra and Stat6 mRNA expression.
source: CXCR3 neutralization in M1 macrophages also slightly increased Il4ra and Stat6 mRNA expression, and increased nuclear localization of active Y641-phosphorylated STAT6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C), which are additional indicators of M2 polarization (Yushi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and citation to Yushi et al., 2016.

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in M1 macrophages increases nuclear localization of pY641-STAT6.
source: CXCR3 neutralization in M1 macrophages also slightly increased Il4ra and Stat6 mRNA expression, and increased nuclear localization of active Y641-phosphorylated STAT6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C), which are additional indicators of M2 polarization (Yushi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and citation to Yushi et al., 2016.

claim: M1-polarized macrophages subjected to CXCR3 inhibition upregulate IRF4.
source: M1-polarized macrophages subjected to CXCR3 inhibition upregulated IRF4, a transcription factor for M2 macrophage polarization, and downregulated the M1 transcription factor IRF5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), indicating a potential mechanism of how pancreatic macrophage populations may shift when CXCR3 is blocked.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: M1-polarized macrophages subjected to CXCR3 inhibition downregulate IRF5.
source: M1-polarized macrophages subjected to CXCR3 inhibition upregulated IRF4, a transcription factor for M2 macrophage polarization, and downregulated the M1 transcription factor IRF5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), indicating a potential mechanism of how pancreatic macrophage populations may shift when CXCR3 is blocked.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in KC mice leads to >50% decrease in inflammatory macrophages.
source: IF-IHC analyses for F4/80+;pY701-STAT1+ cells indicated a >50% decrease in inflammatory macrophages in the CXCR3 NAB-treated mice (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification (Figure 3C,D).

claim: Overall numbers of macrophages remain unchanged after CXCR3 neutralization in KC mice.
source: While overall numbers of macrophages remained unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), IF-IHC analyses for F4/80+;pY701-STAT1+ cells indicated a >50% decrease in inflammatory macrophages in the CXCR3 NAB-treated mice (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in KC mice increases Ym1+ macrophages by approximately threefold.
source: The presence of Ym1+ macrophages in the pancreas was increased by approximately threefold when KC mice were treated with a CXCR3 NAB, as compared to treatment with the isotype control IgG (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC quantification (Figure 4A,B).

claim: CXCL10 neutralization in KC mice increases Ym1+ macrophages.
source: Similar effects on this macrophage population were observed when KC mice were treated with a CXCL10 NAB, as compared to treatment with the isotype control IgG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC quantification (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C).

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in KC mice increases fibrosis.
source: Previously, Ym1+ macrophages in the KC animal model have been shown to drive fibrosis during pancreatic cancer development (Liou et al., 2017), and after neutralization of CXCR3, or alternatively neutralization of CXCL10, we observed a correlating increase in fibrosis (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by SMA staining quantification (Figure 4C,D) and citation to Liou et al., 2017.

claim: CXCL10 neutralization in KC mice increases fibrosis.
source: Previously, Ym1+ macrophages in the KC animal model have been shown to drive fibrosis during pancreatic cancer development (Liou et al., 2017), and after neutralization of CXCR3, or alternatively neutralization of CXCL10, we observed a correlating increase in fibrosis (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by SMA staining quantification (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E) and citation to Liou et al., 2017.

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in KC mice increases abnormal pancreatic areas approximately twofold.
source: In line with increased presence of alternatively activated macrophages and increased fibrosis, abnormal areas (lesions and stroma) increased approximately twofold when KC mice were treated with CXCR3 NAB (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of abnormal areas (Figure 4E,F).

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in non-transgenic mice does not change normal pancreatic tissue.
source: Of note, neutralization of CXCR3 in non-transgenic (ntg) mice did not show any change in the normal pancreatic tissue (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining (Figure 4E).

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in KC mice results in a slight decrease in pancreatic CD3+ cells.
source: After neutralization of CXCR3, we detected a slight (approximately 20%) decrease in pancreatic CD3+ cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), but did not observe any changes in NK (NKG2D+;CD3−) cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) or production of IFNγ (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC quantification (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in KC mice does not change NK cell populations.
source: After neutralization of CXCR3, we detected a slight (approximately 20%) decrease in pancreatic CD3+ cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), but did not observe any changes in NK (NKG2D+;CD3−) cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) or production of IFNγ (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).

claim: CXCR3 neutralization in KC mice does not change IFNγ production.
source: After neutralization of CXCR3, we detected a slight (approximately 20%) decrease in pancreatic CD3+ cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), but did not observe any changes in NK (NKG2D+;CD3−) cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) or production of IFNγ (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH quantification (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).

claim: CXCL10 neutralization in KC mice does not decrease CD3+;CD4+ or CD3+;CD8+ T cells.
source: Moreover, neutralization of CXCL10 did not result in a decrease of CD3+;CD4+ or CD3+;CD8+ T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E).

claim: T-cell depletion does not affect CXCR3 neutralization-induced increase in abnormal pancreatic area.
source: Regardless of T cells being depleted or present (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), CXCR3 neutralization increased abnormal pancreatic area (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C), decreased M1 macrophages (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D), and increased Ym1+ macrophages (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data from T-cell depleted and control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).

claim: T-cell depletion does not affect CXCR3 neutralization-induced decrease in M1 macrophages.
source: Regardless of T cells being depleted or present (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), CXCR3 neutralization increased abnormal pancreatic area (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C), decreased M1 macrophages (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D), and increased Ym1+ macrophages (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data from T-cell depleted and control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).

claim: T-cell depletion does not affect CXCR3 neutralization-induced increase in Ym1+ macrophages.
source: Regardless of T cells being depleted or present (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), CXCR3 neutralization increased abnormal pancreatic area (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C), decreased M1 macrophages (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D), and increased Ym1+ macrophages (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data from T-cell depleted and control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).

claim: T-cell depletion leads to a slight but non-significant decrease in Ifng.
source: Moreover, T-cell depletion led to a slight but non-significant decrease in Ifng, suggesting that T cells are not the only source for IFNγ in this experimental system (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH quantification (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F).

claim: SM3-CXCL10 implanted nude mice have approximately half as much abnormal tissue area as SM3-control implanted mice.
source: Two weeks after implantation, SM3-CXCL10 implanted mice had approximately half as much abnormal tissue area (lesions and fibrosis) as compared to SM3-control implanted mice (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of abnormal areas (Figure 5A,B).

claim: SM3-CXCL10 implanted nude mice show significantly reduced fibrosis compared to SM3-control implanted mice.
source: Analysis of SMA content showed significantly reduced fibrosis in the SM3-CXCL10 implanted mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SMA quantification (Figure 5C).

claim: CXCL10 expression increases the presence of F4/80+ macrophages in nude mice.
source: As expected from the reverse experiment in which we had blocked CXCR3 (Figure 3D), expression of CXCL10 increased the presence of F4/80+ macrophages (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by F4/80 quantification (Figure 5D).

claim: CXCL10 expression increases M1 macrophages and decreases M2 macrophages in nude mice.
source: Further analysis of macrophage polarization types indicated an increase of M1 and a decrease of M2 phenotypes when CXCL10 was present (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of M1 and M2 markers (Figure 5E).

claim: CXCL10 has been previously identified as a chemoattractant for macrophages.
source: In this screen limited to these in vitro lesion cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), besides known factors such as C-C motif chemokine 5 (CCL5) and metalloproteinase inhibitor 1 (TIMP-1), we found strong expression of CXCL10, which has previously been identified as a chemoattractant for macrophages (Tomita et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tomita et al., 2016 and Zhou et al., 2010.

claim: CXCL10 expression has previously been shown to be induced by IFNγ via activation of STAT1.
source: CXCL10 (also IP-10, interferon gamma-inducible protein 10) expression has previously been shown to be induced by interferon gamma (IFNγ) via activation of signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) (Han et al., 2010; Luster and Ravetch, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Han et al., 2010 and Luster and Ravetch, 1987.

claim: T cells and NK cells are known IFNγ producers in the pancreatic microenvironment.
source: T cells and NK cells are known IFNγ producers in the pancreatic microenvironment (Brauner et al., 2010; Chapoval et al., 2001; Loos et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brauner et al., 2010; Chapoval et al., 2001; and Loos et al., 2009.

claim: The influx of macrophages has been demonstrated following injury and during development and progression of pancreatic lesions.
source: With respect to early events leading to development of PDA, the influx of macrophages into the pancreas has been demonstrated following injury and during development and progression of pancreatic lesions (Gea-Sorlí and Closa, 2009; Liou et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gea-Sorlí and Closa, 2009 and Liou et al., 2015.

claim: CXCL10 has been demonstrated as a chemoattractant for macrophages along with other immune cells.
source: Moreover, CXCL10 has been demonstrated as a chemoattractant for macrophages along with other immune cells (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2011.

claim: Ym1 is a bona fide marker for M2 alternatively activated macrophages in precancerous abnormal pancreas lesions.
source: We found that upon CXCR3 neutralization, M1 macrophages, although still iNOS positive, start to express Ym1 (Figure 3A), which we previously have identified as a bona fide marker for M2 alternatively activated macrophages in precancerous abnormal pancreas lesions (Bastea et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bastea et al., 2019.

claim: CD38 is a distinct M1 macrophage marker.
source: A more thorough analysis using qRT-PCR indicated a significant decrease in CD38, which is a distinct M1 macrophage marker (Jablonski et al., 2015), and an upregulation of Ym1, Arg1 and Fizz1 (Figure 3B), which are all markers of the alternatively activated macrophage population that previously has been shown to drive fibrosis during pancreatic lesion progression (Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jablonski et al., 2015.

claim: Ym1, Arg1, and Fizz1 are markers of the alternatively activated macrophage population that drive fibrosis during pancreatic lesion progression.
source: A more thorough analysis using qRT-PCR indicated a significant decrease in CD38, which is a distinct M1 macrophage marker (Jablonski et al., 2015), and an upregulation of Ym1, Arg1 and Fizz1 (Figure 3B), which are all markers of the alternatively activated macrophage population that previously has been shown to drive fibrosis during pancreatic lesion progression (Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liou et al., 2017.

claim: Ym1+ macrophages in the KC animal model have been shown to drive fibrosis during pancreatic cancer development.
source: Previously, Ym1+ macrophages in the KC animal model have been shown to drive fibrosis during pancreatic cancer development (Liou et al., 2017), and after neutralization of CXCR3, or alternatively neutralization of CXCL10, we observed a correlating increase in fibrosis (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liou et al., 2017.

claim: Cxcr3−/− mice show an abundance of M2 macrophages in breast tumors.
source: Our data is in line with a recent study in which it was reported that Cxcr3−/− mice show an abundance of M2 macrophages in breast tumors (Oghumu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Oghumu et al., 2014.

claim: Cxcr3−/− macrophages have reduced ability to upregulate iNOS and show a predisposition for M2 polarization.
source: Specifically, similar to what we observed after CXCR3 neutralization, Cxcr3−/− macrophages from these mice had reduced ability to upregulate iNOS and showed a predisposition for M2 polarization (Oghumu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Oghumu et al., 2014.

claim: CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling axis has been implicated in generating inflammation in various diseases including pancreatitis.
source: The CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling axis has been implicated in generating inflammation in various diseases including pancreatitis (Lee et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2011; and Singh et al., 2007.

claim: Gastric cancer patients with upregulated CXCR3 expression showed better survival.
source: With respect to cancer, gastric cancer patients with upregulated CXCR3 expression showed better survival (Chen et al., 2019; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2019 and Li et al., 2015.

claim: High expression of CXCL10 and other CXCR3 ligands in ovarian, esophageal, and non-small cell lung carcinoma indicate favorable prognoses.
source: Also, high expression of CXCL10 and other CXCR3 ligands in ovarian, esophageal, and non-small cell lung carcinoma indicate favorable prognoses (Bronger et al., 2016; Cao et al., 2017; Sato et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bronger et al., 2016; Cao et al., 2017; and Sato et al., 2016.

claim: In pancreatic cancer, expression of both CXCL10 and CXCR3 in tumor tissue has been correlated with poor prognosis.
source: In contrast, in pancreatic cancer, expression of both CXCL10 and CXCR3 in tumor tissue has been correlated with a poor prognosis (Liu et al., 2011; Lunardi et al., 2014) mostly due to increased chemoresistance (Delitto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2011; Lunardi et al., 2014; and Delitto et al., 2015.

claim: CXCL10 upregulation in chronic pancreatitis patients occurs in the absence of oncogenic mutations.
source: This finding is supported by other studies that have shown CXCL10 upregulation in chronic pancreatitis patients, which occurs in the absence of oncogenic mutations (Singh et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2007.

claim: Inflammatory macrophages are predominantly located at ADM lesions, driving the transdifferentiation process.
source: During pancreatic cancer development, inflammatory macrophages are predominantly located at ADM lesions, driving the transdifferentiation process (Liou et al., 2015; Liou et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liou et al., 2015 and Liou et al., 2013.

claim: PanIN1 lesions express the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-13 (IL-13), which causes a polarization shift from M1 toward an alternatively activated, Ym1+ phenotype.
source: More progressed PanIN1 lesions have been shown to express the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-13 (IL-13), which causes a polarization shift from M1 toward an alternatively activated, Ym1+ phenotype (Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liou et al., 2017.

claim: In pancreatic cancer, expression of both CXCL10 and CXCR3 in tumor tissue have been correlated with metastasis and poor prognosis.
source: However, it needs to be noted that in pancreatic cancer expression of both CXCL10 and CXCR3 in tumor tissue have been correlated with metastasis and poor prognosis (Cannon et al., 2020; Hirth et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2011; Lunardi et al., 2014; Romero et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cannon et al., 2020; Hirth et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2011; Lunardi et al., 2014; and Romero et al., 2020.

claim: SM3 cells form lesions with PanIN features when cultivated on extracellular matrix.
source: Therefore, we used SM3 cells, which have been isolated from the precancerous epithelium of a KC mouse and form lesions with PanIN features when cultivated on extracellular matrix (Agbunag et al., 2006; Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Agbunag et al., 2006 and Liou et al., 2017.

claim: SM3 cells express CCL5 and TIMP-1.
source: In this screen limited to these in vitro lesion cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), besides known factors such as C-C motif chemokine 5 (CCL5) and metalloproteinase inhibitor 1 (TIMP-1), we found strong expression of CXCL10, which has previously been identified as a chemoattractant for macrophages (Tomita et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytokine array data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) most likely originates from precancerous pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasm (PanIN) lesions.
source: Genetic mouse models have shown that pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) most likely originates from precancerous pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasm (PanIN) lesions (reviewed in Storz, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Storz, 2017.

claim: The development and progression of PanIN lesions is dependent on crosstalk between a multitude of host cells in their microenvironment.
source: The development and progression of these early lesions is dependent on crosstalk between a multitude of host cells in their microenvironment.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Inflammatory (M1-polarized) and alternatively activated (M2-polarized) macrophages are the most consequential cell types in the PanIN microenvironment.
source: Of these, inflammatory (M1-polarized) and alternatively activated (M2-polarized) macrophages are the most consequential cell types.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The initial influx of macrophages occurs in response to an aberrant release of chemokines from pancreatic cells undergoing transformation.
source: The initial influx of macrophages, which induces local inflammation, occurs in response to an aberrant release of chemokines from pancreatic cells undergoing transformation (Liou et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liou et al., 2015.

claim: Local inflammation alone is not an efficient driver of oncogenic progression.
source: However, local inflammation alone is not an efficient driver of oncogenic progression and requires additional inflammatory signaling, genetic alterations, and downregulation of factors that maintain acinar cell identity (Carrière et al., 2011; Cobo et al., 2018; Guerra et al., 2011; Guerra et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carrière et al., 2011; Cobo et al., 2018; Guerra et al., 2011; and Guerra et al., 2007.

claim: Inflammatory macrophages contribute to pre-neoplastic lesion formation via secretion of inflammatory mediators.
source: Inflammatory macrophages contribute to pre-neoplastic lesion formation via secretion of inflammatory mediators, which regulate reorganization of the acinar microenvironment and initiate acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM) (Liou et al., 2015; Liou et al., 2013; Sawey et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liou et al., 2015; Liou et al., 2013; and Sawey et al., 2007.

claim: Pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages are important for the initiation of precancerous lesions.
source: While pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages are important for the initiation of precancerous lesions, this population dwindles and M2 macrophages become more predominant (Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liou et al., 2017.

claim: M2 macrophages are Ym1/Chil3, Arg1, Retnla, and IL-1ra positive.
source: These M2 macrophages are chitinase-like protein 3 (Ym1/Chil3), arginase-1 (Arg1), resistin-like alpha (Fizz1/Retnla), and interleukin-1 receptor antagonist protein (IL-1ra) positive and promote lesion growth, drive fibrogenesis, and block T-cell infiltration (Bastea et al., 2019; Liou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bastea et al., 2019 and Liou et al., 2017.

claim: Alternatively activated macrophages represent approximately 85% of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) in pancreatic tumors.

claim: Tissue-resident macrophages shape fibrotic responses in full-blown pancreatic cancer.
source: For full-blown pancreatic cancer, tissue-resident macrophages have been suggested to shape fibrotic responses (Zhu et al., 2017), while infiltrating monocytes generate an immunosuppressive environment (Zhang et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: Infiltrating monocytes generate an immunosuppressive environment in full-blown pancreatic cancer.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2017 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: CXCL10 acts through its cognate receptor CXCR3.
source: C-X-C motif chemokine 10 (CXCL10), also known as IFNγ-induced protein 10 (IP-10), acts through its cognate receptor C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 3 (CXCR3) (Groom and Luster, 2011) and regulates the chemotaxis of CXCR3+ immune cells such as macrophages, T cells, and natural killer (NK) cells (Luster and Ravetch, 1987; Tomita et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Groom and Luster, 2011.

claim: Both CXCL10 and CXCR3 are expressed in pancreatic cancer tumor tissue.
source: In pancreatic cancer, both CXCL10 and CXCR3 are expressed in tumor tissue (Delitto et al., 2015), and their presence has been correlated with poor prognosis (Liu et al., 2011; Lunardi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Delitto et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2011; and Lunardi et al., 2014.

claim: The fibrotic microenvironment of pancreatic cancer acts as a barrier for delivery of tumor cell targeting drugs.
source: Pancreatic cancer is difficult to target because its fibrotic microenvironment not only acts as a barrier for delivery of tumor cell targeting drugs, but it also generates an anti-inflammatory environment and prevents immunotherapy (Balachandran et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Balachandran et al., 2019.

claim: The fibrotic microenvironment of pancreatic cancer generates an anti-inflammatory environment and prevents immunotherapy.

claim: One current paradigm for treatment of PDA focuses on combining chemotherapy with immune modulators that reprogram tumor-promoting macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype.
source: One of the current paradigms for treatment of PDA focuses on combining chemotherapy with immune modulators that reprogram tumor-promoting macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype (Bastea et al., 2019; Mitchem et al., 2013; Pandey and Storz, 2019).
